content: There is therefore now no condemnation to those who are in Christ Jesus, who don’t walk according to the flesh, but according to the Spirit. {{v:2}} For the law of the Spirit of life in Christ Jesus made me free from the law of sin and of death. {{v:3}} For what the law couldn’t do, in that it was weak through the flesh, God did, sending his own Son in the likeness of sinful flesh and for sin, he condemned sin in the flesh, {{v:4}} that the ordinance of the law might be fulfilled in us who don’t walk according to the flesh, but according to the Spirit. {{v:5}} For those who live according to the flesh set their minds on the things of the flesh, but those who live according to the Spirit, the things of the Spirit. {{v:6}} For the mind of the flesh is death, but the mind of the Spirit is life and peace; {{v:7}} because the mind of the flesh is hostile toward God, for it is not subject to God’s law, neither indeed can it be. {{v:8}} Those who are in the flesh can’t please God. {{v:9}} But you are not in the flesh but in the Spirit, if it is so that the Spirit of God dwells in you. But if any man doesn’t have the Spirit of Christ, he is not his. {{v:10}} If Christ is in you, the body is dead because of sin, but the spirit is alive because of righteousness. {{v:11}} But if the Spirit of him who raised up Jesus from the dead dwells in you, he who raised up Christ Jesus from the dead will also give life to your mortal bodies through his Spirit who dwells in you.

facets.text: Paul opens with the triumphant declaration that there is no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus. This freedom is not merely a legal acquittal but a new state of existence: the believer is united to Christ and set free by 'the law of the Spirit of life' from 'the law of sin and of death.' The Christian's standing before God rests entirely on incorporation into Christ, not on personal achievement under the old order.
facets.question: What does it mean that there is no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus?

facets.text: The Mosaic Law was holy yet powerless to save because it was 'weak through the flesh'—it could reveal and demand righteousness but could not supply the strength to fulfill it. What the Law could not accomplish, God did by sending his own Son. This distinguishes the Law's diagnostic function from the grace of redemption, which alone conquers sin at its root.
facets.question: Why couldn't the Law save us, and what did God do that the Law could not?

facets.text: God's Son came 'in the likeness of sinful flesh and for sin,' and in that flesh 'he condemned sin.' Christ assumed a truly human nature like ours in every way but sin, and in his own body—especially in his sacrificial death—he passed judgment on sin itself. This is the mystery of the Incarnation ordered to atonement: the Word becomes flesh precisely to defeat sin in the very sphere where it had reigned.
facets.question: How did Christ condemn sin in the flesh through the Incarnation?

facets.text: The purpose of Christ's redeeming work is that 'the ordinance of the law might be fulfilled in us who walk according to the Spirit.' Grace does not abolish the moral demand of the Law but empowers its true fulfillment from within by the Holy Spirit. The Christian life is thus the Law's righteous requirement realized through interior transformation rather than mere external observance.
facets.question: Does the grace of Christ free us from the Law or fulfill it in us?

facets.text: Paul sets flesh and Spirit against each other as two opposed orientations of the whole person. The mind of the flesh is death because it is hostile to God and cannot submit to his law, while the mind of the Spirit is 'life and peace.' This is not a contempt for the body but a description of the fundamental choice between self-centered rebellion and Spirit-led communion with God.
facets.question: What is the difference between living according to the flesh and living according to the Spirit?

facets.text: The indwelling of the Holy Spirit is the mark that identifies who belongs to Christ: 'if any man doesn't have the Spirit of Christ, he is not his.' The Spirit of God, the Spirit of Christ, dwells within the baptized as an interior presence, making the believer genuinely Christ's own. Christian identity is therefore constituted by this indwelling gift, not by outward affiliation alone.
facets.question: How does the indwelling of the Holy Spirit show that we belong to Christ?

facets.text: The same Spirit who raised Jesus from the dead and dwells in believers guarantees that God 'will also give life to your mortal bodies.' The resurrection is not only a past event about Christ but a promise reaching to the believer's own body. Because the Spirit already indwells us, the future bodily resurrection is assured as the completion of the life we now possess in seed.
facets.question: How does the Spirit who raised Jesus assure the resurrection of our own bodies?

facets.text: The passage is thoroughly Trinitarian: the Father sends his own Son and raises him from the dead, the Son condemns sin in his flesh, and the Spirit of both dwells within and gives life. Our salvation is the shared work of the three divine Persons, drawing the believer into the very life of the Trinity through indwelling and communion.
facets.question: How does salvation involve the work of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit together?

merged.annotation:
SUMMARY: Romans 8:1–11 proclaims freedom from condemnation for those in Christ, contrasts life in the flesh with life in the Spirit, and grounds present justification and future bodily resurrection in the Trinitarian work of salvation and the indwelling Holy Spirit.

[DOCTRINAL | explicit]: No condemnation for those in Christ Jesus; freedom by the law of the Spirit of life from the law of sin and death through union with Christ.
[SCRIPTURAL | explicit]: The Law was holy but powerless through the flesh; what it could not do, God accomplished by sending his Son.
[DOCTRINAL | traditional]: The Incarnation ordered to atonement—the Son sent in the likeness of sinful flesh condemned sin in the flesh, true man yet sinless.
[MORAL | traditional]: Grace does not abolish but fulfills the righteous requirement of the Law within those who walk by the Spirit through interior transformation.
[MORAL | explicit]: Flesh versus Spirit as opposed orientations of the whole person; the mind of the flesh is death and hostility to God, the Spirit is life and peace.
[DOCTRINAL | explicit]: The indwelling Spirit of Christ constitutes belonging to Christ; without the Spirit one is not his.
[DOCTRINAL | explicit]: The Spirit who raised Jesus assures the future resurrection and life of the believer's mortal body.
[DOCTRINAL | inferential]: The Trinitarian structure of salvation—Father sends and raises, Son condemns sin, Spirit indwells and gives life—draws believers into communion with the Trinity.
